c.v: Evolving Medtigo from a single-provider tool into a unified platform for hospitals and healthcare providers to manage credentials, licenses, certificates, renewals, and new license applications. I redesigned the existing Provider View and created a new Admin View for hospitals and organisations.
Medtigo simplifies provider management by bringing licensing, credential monitoring, compliance, billing, and education into one unified platform.
Used by providers, hospitals, and organisations working with Medtigo, with access based on assigned permissions.
The existing single-user experience, rebuilt around one consistent pattern.
A new layer for hospitals and organisations to manage all their providers.
Understanding that the business needed more than the existing platform.
The previous platform worked for a single provider only, so hospitals could not manage their providers together.
Medtigo’s analyst team tracked licenses and credentials with spreadsheets and emails.
CME/CE, billing and educational information were not covered, and the navigation did not reflect all of Medtigo’s businesses.
The interface was visually weak and several user flows had problems.
The old platform was affecting the business, so stakeholders needed the redesign as soon as possible.
How might we turn a single-provider tool into one platform where hospitals manage all their providers, and providers can follow every license application from start to finish?
How each role uses the platform, and what they need from it.
Know which provider credentials need attention, and keep every provider’s information in one place.
Find providers, monitor licenses and certificates, track applications, review CME/CE compliance, export reports, handle invoices.
Keep credentials current, apply for new licenses, and complete what is needed to get licensed.
Order a service, track acquisition tasks, start renewals, view certificates and course activity.
Move each application forward on the provider’s behalf.
Assign and review tasks and notes on license applications.
Understand the business gap: a single-provider tool versus organisation-level needs.
Review the existing flows and navigation to find what blocked the business.
Define one module structure for both views, with entry points for each role.
Redesign the provider acquisition flow first, the most complex journey.
Design the new Admin View on the same pattern.
Build reusable components so both views stayed consistent under a tight deadline.
Both views share one module pattern. The Admin View is organised around providers and reports; the provider view around personal activity.
The provider acquisition flow was the most complex journey. The Admin View flows build on the same modules.

c.v: Wireframes that explain the layout logic behind the final screens.
Admin View first, then the provider view.
One dashboard answers “what needs my attention first?”: a needs-attention strip, credential health by type, upcoming expirations, the acquisition pipeline, tasks, and the providers that need action.
Design decision: lead with what needs action, then show the evidence behind it.
A searchable directory leads to a provider profile, where documents, monitoring and acquisition each have their own tab.
Design decision: keep one provider’s information in one place without crowding a single screen.
Monitoring lists every credential with priority, progress and an auto-renewal switch. Acquisition shows each application’s tasks and timeline.
Design decision: one table pattern with a single clear action per row (Start Renewal or View Details).
CME/CE compliance can be read per provider, per state or per subject, with a direct Take Course action. Reports can be filtered and exported, with a history of past exports.
Design decision: show the gap and the next step side by side.
Invoices, invoice details and balance history sit in one module.

A personal dashboard leads with what needs the provider’s attention: expired and at-risk credentials, pending tasks and course credits. Renewals, applications, courses and certificates follow, with Order Service always within reach.
Design decision: put credentials to renew first, ordered by priority.
Provider view: applying for a license and tracking it
The most complex journey: apply for a new license, then follow every task and stage until approval.
Design decision: tasks carry their own action (Sign, Complete, Fill Form), and a timeline shows the current stage.
Providers can order known services across states, or ask for a consultation.
Design decision: two clear paths in one window, with “What happens next?” to set expectations.

A redesigned provider experience, including the license application and tracking flow.
One consistent set of patterns and components across both views.
Scaling a single-user tool to organisations is mostly an information structure problem.
Reusing one table and filter pattern made a large product feasible on a tight deadline.
A flow that ends with a clear next action matters more than a good-looking list.
